groups.text: A payment is captured.
Now three messages go out: an email, an SMS and a push notification.
Each one is an async child of one coroutineScope, and each async hands back a Deferred: a box for its result.
At fifty milliseconds the SMS call throws.
Nobody has called await yet.
What happens to the email?
The failure goes up at once.
A failed child tells its parent the moment it fails, and that is true for async too.
Nothing waits in the Deferred.
The parent cancels the email and the push, and coroutineScope throws the SMS exception to the caller.
The customer gets nothing.
But these messages don't need each other.
An SMS outage should not stop the email.
So give them a parent that lets a child fail alone.
Same failure. Where does it go now?
It stays with the child.
The parent doesn't cancel anyone, and the exception waits in the SMS Deferred.
The push is sent at one hundred milliseconds, and the email at three hundred.
Later the block calls await.
Each Deferred hands back what it holds, and for the SMS, await rethrows the IOException, where a try can catch it.
This parent is a supervisor: here, supervisorScope.
Its children fail alone, but cancelling it still stops every child.
With launch there is no Deferred.
A failed launch child of a supervisor hands its exception to the CoroutineExceptionHandler in its context, which can only log it.
Put that handler on a child of a plain parent, and it is never called: the child tells its parent first.
A handler works only at a root, or on a direct child of a supervisor.
This is Kotlin only.
Write supervisorScope inside a function, or put SupervisorJob and the handler in the constructor of a scope you own.
So a plain parent sends a failure up at once.
A supervisor keeps it with the child: in the Deferred for async, in the handler for launch.
Quick check. A launch child of coroutineScope has its own handler, and it throws.
Who gets the exception?
